## The situation

Within days of the M7.5 quake (24 June 2026), **eight+ organisations** published satellite
building-damage maps — government (Copernicus), academic radar (OSU, IMPACT), optical AI
(Microsoft, U. Houston, WFP/LIST), debris models (UNEP), volunteer AI (HOT, DISHA).

They **disagreed with each other, sometimes wildly.** A coordinator had no principled way to
answer: *which do I trust, for what, and at what scale?*

::: {.tldr}
**What we did** — scored the six products that published an analysed extent against **three
reference datasets whose blind spots don't overlap**, so they check each other and the products.
:::

::: {.tldr}
**Bottom line** — as delivered, most single products carried **less usable per-building
information than a no-satellite baseline**. But they *are* good at ranking neighbourhoods,
combining helps within limits, and the real leverage is **reference quality + provider
transparency**.
:::

## Three questions — kept strictly separate

::: {.tldr}
**1 · Where is it worst?** — ranking neighbourhoods for triage.
**2 · Which buildings?** — a list you could send a crew to.
**3 · What does everyone miss?** — including the "ground truth" itself.
:::

And two performance frames we **never mix**:

- **Best case** — Caraballeda, the dense-damage zone where **96% of the expert reference
  lives.** Where most published numbers implicitly come from.
- **As delivered** — the whole product, every zone it shipped, junk included. What a
  responder actually received.

<p class="big">That split is itself a finding.</p>

## The three references — who they are {.smaller}

![](artefacts/RQ0-matching-basis/figs/reference_architecture.png)

::: {.notes}
Read this before anything else. Two HOT datasets, confusingly named: MapSwipe = REMOTE
VOLUNTEERS voting on AI-flagged ~50m hex cells (NOT building points) — it sharpens PRECISION
by adjudicating flags, but its verdict is per-cell so the 0.24 is an upper estimate. ChatMap =
FIELD TEAMS reporting building-level points from the ground — it extends RECALL inland and
can union with CEMS points (+5-9%). CEMS = the expert points, anchors both sides. They're
used SEPARATELY because their blind spots don't overlap.
:::

## Method — one line

::: {.tldr}
Matching is **dual-anchored** — precision and recall from opposite anchors, so we never count
the vast stock of undamaged buildings. Radius r = 10 m, set by the urban fabric (median
building spacing 9.7 m). **Target throughout: buildings the expert graded *damaged or
destroyed* (CEMS classes 2–3)** — not destruction alone.
:::

## How matching works

![](artefacts/RQ0-matching-basis/figs/fig_dual_anchor_matching.png)

::: {.notes}
Left: score only where product AND reference both looked. Middle: recall — each real damage
point asks "is there a flag within r?". Right: precision — each flag asks "is there a real
damage point within r?". Opposite anchors, so no true-negative count needed.
:::

## Their most useful capability — ranking neighbourhoods {.smaller}

![](artefacts/RQ3-prioritization-error-structure/figs/rq3_priority_map.png)

<p style="text-align:center; font-size:0.8em;">Rank correlation with real damage
**ρ ≈ 0.5–0.6** — moderate, and better than their per-building skill.</p>

::: {.notes}
Cells shaded by REAL damage (CEMS damaged-or-destroyed count); blue outline = product's own
top-10 worst-hit picks. Both get 6/10 — vs ~3 expected by chance, so a real but MODEST signal.
The robust number is rank correlation rho 0.5-0.6. HONEST CAVEATS to hold: (1) best-case
Caraballeda, coarse scale — finer ranking degrades; (2) we have NOT yet checked whether the
day-zero geography baseline ranks areas equally well — it plausibly does, since the damage
gradient IS the coast/shaking gradient. So present this as "products' most useful capability,"
NOT as a clean win over the free baseline. Don't quote a top-N percentage in the room.
:::

## Where they struggle — the per-building list

Target: **damaged *or* destroyed** buildings (expert classes 2–3). In Caraballeda, where
products score highest:

<p class="big">precision 0.04 – 0.09</p>

Counting **only expert-recorded damage**, for every flag that hits, **10–20 miss.**
*(Crediting damage the expert missed — from crowd/field data — cuts this to ~4–5; see the
operating-cost slide. Same buildings, stricter vs. fairer scoring.)*

::: {.tldr}
The benchmark that should worry us: a model given **only day-zero geography** — coast
distance, building density, ShakeMap intensity, all available *before any satellite is
tasked* — matches the best single product.
:::

## The benchmark that should give us pause

![](artefacts/RQ8-learned-fusion/figs/rq8b_asdelivered_bars.png)

::: {.notes}
Two bars per product: light = best case (scored only in the common area ≈ Caraballeda, where
all products AND the day-zero baseline see the same buildings); dark = as delivered (over the
product's full shipped footprint). Red line = the no-satellite day-zero baseline in the common
area (0.08), a single number since it's one area. Story: in the best zone every product merely
TIES the baseline; as delivered most fall BELOW it. Microsoft holds only because it shipped
just its best zone — coverage restraint is a virtue. Caveat: as-delivered bars are on full
footprints where the reference is thin, so that penalty leans on sparse reference; but a
responder faced the same deficit. AP = one number summarising the whole precision-recall curve.
:::

## The reference has its own blind spot {.smaller}

<p style="text-align:center; font-size:0.75em; color:#52514e;">Recall vs the **415 ChatMap
field reports** · grades: *complete / significant* · every row (incl. CEMS) scored against
the ground</p>

![](artefacts/RQ2-cems-footprint-points/figs/rq2e_grade_slope.png)

::: {.notes}
Scoring Copernicus against the field reports: 94% of COMPLETE destruction found, but only 49%
of SIGNIFICANT damage. Every product shows the same downward slope (this panel = recall vs
ChatMap field grades). So: (1) satellite damage detection is really destruction detection —
shelter needs under-counted; (2) measured precision is a FLOOR, measured recall is a CEILING.
MapSwipe volunteers lift Microsoft's precision 0.08 -> ~0.24 — the gap is in the reference, not
the product.
:::

## The destruction bias shows in precision too {.smaller}

<p style="text-align:center; font-size:0.75em; color:#52514e;">Different validation set:
vs **CEMS's own 1,467 points** · grades: *Damaged / Destroyed* · numbers not comparable to
the previous slide — the shared message is the slope</p>

![](artefacts/RQ2-cems-footprint-points/figs/rq2l_grade_pr.png)

::: {.notes}
Companion to the previous slide, but on the EXPERT's own grades (Damaged class 2 vs Destroyed
class 3), so precision is well-defined (field data too sparse for precision). Both panels: every
product finds/flags Destroyed better than Damaged. Steep lines = destruction-biased (MS, UH,
UNEP — appearance/debris). Flat lines = grade-neutral (OSU, IMPACT radar coherence — they sense
structural change, not just visible collapse; LIST sides with them, so it's a tendency not a
clean optical-vs-radar law). This is why the ecosystem under-serves shelter (lighter-damage)
needs — confirmed on both metrics, from the expert reference itself.
:::

## One product is many scorecards

![](artefacts/RQ2-cems-footprint-points/figs/rq2i_per_aoi_scorecard.png)

::: {.notes}
96% of reference damage in Caraballeda (first column = pooled/as-delivered). Outside it,
products keep flagging at scale (UH: 32k flags in Santa Cruz) while measured precision collapses
to 0.00-0.02 — BUT we cannot separate "product hallucination" from "reference too thin" there.
Honest verdict: every headline number describes dense-damage coastal terrain.
:::

## Even within one product, performance flips across the coast {.smaller}

![](artefacts/RQ2-cems-footprint-points/figs/rq2j_deck_ms_hex.png)

::: {.notes}
Microsoft, its full coastal extent, res-7 cells. Top: precision — dark = trustworthy flags,
pale = mostly false alarms. Bottom: field visits per real damaged building found (reversed
scale, dark = cheap/good). The WEST end is pale/expensive (the single-scene over-flagged
cluster), the EAST end trustworthy/cheap. Same product, opposite verdicts by location — which
is why a single product-level number misleads.
:::

## Precision across Caraballeda, by product (1/2) {.smaller}

![](artefacts/RQ2-cems-footprint-points/figs/rq2j_caraballeda_p1.png)

::: {.notes}
All three on the SAME scale, zoomed to the dense-damage zone. MS has the most dark
(high-precision) cells, concentrated in the east; IMPACT lighter; OSU palest (it floods flags
→ high recall but low precision everywhere). Grey = <20 flags in that cell. Even here, in the
best zone, no product is uniformly trustworthy.
:::

## Precision across Caraballeda, by product (2/2) {.smaller}

![](artefacts/RQ2-cems-footprint-points/figs/rq2j_caraballeda_p2.png)

::: {.notes}
UH, LIST, UNEP, same scale as the previous slide. All pale — low per-cell precision throughout
even in the dense zone. Recall and F1 versions of every product are in the register if wanted.
:::

## Does combining products fix it? Partly.

![](artefacts/RQ5-ensemble/figs/rq5c_operational_dial.png)

::: {.notes}
Each bar spans the honest cost range: TOP = strict (only expert-recorded damage counts — this
is the "10-20 per hit" from the earlier slide); BOTTOM square/dot = best estimate (also counts
damage the expert missed, crowd-confirmed). Same buildings, two scorings. Agreement trades
precision vs coverage: at ~4-of-6 you reach 74% of damaged-or-destroyed buildings at ~3-5
visits per find; full agreement is nearly clean but covers a quarter. No rule is both cheap and
complete — a prioritisation DIAL, not a work order. The dial itself is the value single
products don't give: each product hands you one fixed point.
:::

## Transparency lets you fix failures

![](artefacts/RQ7-mapswipe-validation/figs/rq7_west_cluster_adjudication.png)

::: {.notes}
Microsoft's one bad zone (western strip) flagged 28.7% of buildings; crowd rejected 71% as
undamaged. We root-caused it FROM MICROSOFT'S OWN METADATA: single satellite pass, per-scene
model, no cross-check. It was the ONLY failure we could diagnose — the only product publishing
per-building provenance. Auditability is a product property. And the correction signal (the
crowd campaign) existed within days and reached no one.
:::

## What we'd recommend

::: {.tldr}
**Providers** — publish an analysed extent (non-negotiable); publish per-building provenance
(scene count + dates); *scope* your coverage rather than blanket-ship; clear a geography-only
baseline before release.
:::

::: {.tldr}
**Evaluators** — one expert reference under-counts light damage. Publish precision as a
*floor*, or adjudicate against a second reference and publish an *interval*. Crowd and field
data are first-class, not afterthoughts.
:::

::: {.tldr}
**Responders** — trust the *area ranking*, not the building counts; set the agreement dial to
your own cost of a wasted visit vs. a missed building. Nothing here sees light damage reliably
— plan shelter assessments accordingly.
:::

## Where this is solid — and where it isn't

**Solid** — six products, three independent references, ~1,500 lines of reproducible open
code. The area-ranking win, the day-zero result, the per-zone collapse, and the west-cluster
diagnosis all hold across frames.

**Honest limits:**

- **One event, one geography** (coastal, dense-urban); 96% of reference in one AOI.
- Outside Caraballeda the reference is too thin to cleanly separate product error from
  reference gaps — the as-delivered penalty leans on that.
- **No confidence intervals yet** — needed before leaning on the ±0.01 gaps.
- The **timeliness axis** (accuracy × how fast each product arrived) isn't built yet —
  arguably the most decision-relevant variable.

## The asks

::: {.ask}
**1 · Back writing this up.** The framework — three-reference triangulation, the floor/ceiling
correction, the geography baseline as a validation bar — is novel and travels beyond this event.
:::

::: {.ask}
**2 · Support taking findings to providers.** Constructive and evidence-based; their own
metadata is the hero. This strengthens the ecosystem, doesn't just critique it.
:::

::: {.ask}
**3 · Resource the two gaps that make it bulletproof** — confidence intervals, and the
timeliness axis (needs provider release dates, an ask we can make together).
:::

## One line to carry out of the room

<p class="big" style="line-height:1.4; font-size:1.25em;">As delivered, most single damage
products barely beat a coastline-and-shakemap model.<br>Their value is in ranking areas and in
combination — and the biggest lever is better reference data and provider transparency, not
better single models.</p>
